title: Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd vs Hari Chand on 31 July, 2025
full_text: Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd vs Hari Chand on 31 July, 2025 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand IN THE COURT OF JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE FIRST CLASS(NI ACT-02), SOUTH EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURT COMPLEX, NEW DELHI (Presided over by Ms. Shruti Sharma-I) DLSE020110602015 Criminal Complaint No.:630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. ....................Complainant Vs. Name and address of Mr. Hari Chand S/o Late Rambat R/o House the Accused. no. 6, Shree Chand Sarpanch Wali Gali, Village-Sungarpur,Narela,Delhi-1000036 C. Offence complained of U/s 138 NIAct D. Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHARMA SHRUTI Date: Page no.1/25 SHARMA 2025.07.31 16:34:39 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand JUDGMENT 1. By way of the present judgment, I proceed to adjudicate and dispose of the complaint instituted by M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Limited, now known as Saral Home Finance Limited (hereinafter referred to as "the complainant"), a duly incorporated housing finance company registered under the Companies Act, 1956 , and represented through its duly authorized representative. The complaint has been filed against Shri Hari Chand, son of Late Ram Pat (hereinafter referred to as "the accused"), alleging commission of the offence punishable under Section 138 read with Section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as "the NI Act "). The proceedings arise out of the alleged dishonor of cheque bearing no. 013354 dated 03.09.2012, drawn by the accused on Bank of India, Bakhtawarpur Branch, New Delhi, for an amount of ₹9,39,030/-, issued in favour of the complainant towards discharge of outstanding dues under a housing loan sanctioned to the accused. The dishonour of the said cheque on the ground of 'Funds Insufficient' has given rise to the present cause of action. 2. It has been specifically averred by the complainant that the accused, along with a co-applicant, had approached the complainant institution for a housing loan and was sanctioned a sum of ₹10,00,000/- vide sanction letter dated 24.05.2011, for renovation of a residential property situated at Khasra No. 1061, Village Barula, Tehsil Dadri, District Gautam Budh Nagar, Uttar Pradesh. Pursuant to the sanction, the accused executed a loan agreement dated 02.06.2011, wherein he agreed to repay the loan in 144 equated monthly installments of ₹17,386/- each over a period of 12 years. The terms and conditions governing the repayment were duly accepted by the accused at the Page no.2/25 Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:34:43 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand time of execution of the said loan documents. 3. It is alleged by the complainant that the accused began defaulting in the repayment of monthly installments in violation of the agreed terms of the loan agreement. Despite repeated reminders and issuance of a demand letter dated 24.08.2012, whereby the accused was called upon to clear the arrears failing which the complainant would be constrained to recall the entire outstanding loan amount, the accused failed to respond or regularize the overdue payments. Consequently, the complainant was compelled to recall the entire loan and initiate recovery proceedings. 4. It is the case of the complainant that in discharge of his outstanding liability towards the recalled loan amount, the accused issued cheque bearing no. 013354 dated 03.09.2012 for a sum of ₹9,39,030/-, drawn on Bank of India, Bakhtawarpur Branch, New Delhi-110036. However, to the complainant's dismay, upon presentation of the said cheque through its banker, Punjab National Bank, Nehru Place Branch, New Delhi, the cheque was returned unpaid vide cheque return memo dated 07.09.2012 with the endorsement "Funds Insufficient". 5. Upon being informed by the complainant about the dishonour of the aforementioned cheque on account of insufficient funds, the accused allegedly failed to offer any satisfactory explanation or justification for the same and did not make good the payment. The complainant has thus alleged that by issuing a cheque which was returned unpaid due to insufficiency of funds, the accused has committed an offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 6. This deliberate default, coupled with the dishonour of the cheque due to insufficiency of funds, has led the complainant to contend that the accused Page no.3/25 Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:34:46 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand had no bona fide intention to honour his financial obligations. The complainant asserts that the issuance of the cheque, followed by its dishonour, reflects a willful breach of legal liability on part of the accused, thereby attracting penal consequences under the provisions of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 7. Subsequent to the dishonour of the cheque, and in adherence to the statutory requirements enshrined under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, the complainant, through its engaged counsel, caused to be issued a legal demand notice dated 26.09.2012, which was dispatched to the accused via Registered Post with Acknowledgement Due (AD). Through the said notice, the accused was unequivocally called upon to pay the dishonoured cheque amount of ₹9,39,030/- within the prescribed statutory period of fifteen days from the date of receipt. The legal notice was addressed to the residential address of the accused, as furnished in the loan documents and reiterated in the body of the complaint. 8. As per the postal records and acknowledgment card placed on record, the notice was duly served upon the accused on 29.09.2012. However, despite the service of the legal notice and the lapse of the mandatory statutory period, the accused neither made the payment of the cheque amount nor issued any written reply or response controverting the liability. The deliberate failure of the accused to comply with the legal demand notice, even after the dishonour of the cheque, prompted the complainant to invoke the penal provisions of the NI Act . Accordingly, the complainant instituted the present complaint under Sections 138 and 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, seeking penal consequences against the accused for wilful default and for the enforcement of the statutory presumption of liability arising from the dishonoured negotiable instrument. 9. Upon a careful perusal of the material placed on record along with Page no.4/25 Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:34:49 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand the complaint, and after due examination of the complainant's authorised representative by way of pre-summoning evidence in accordance with the mandate of Section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, this Court was satisfied that a prima facie case was made out against the accused for the commission of an offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The evidence adduced at the pre-summoning stage sufficiently disclosed the existence of a legally enforceable liability and the issuance of the cheque in question by the accused towards its discharge, followed by its dishonour due to insufficiency of funds. Accordingly, vide order dated 02.06.2016, this Court was pleased to take cognizance of the offence and summoned the accused to face trial for the alleged dishonour of cheque issued in discharge of a debt or liability, as contemplated under the statutory scheme of the NI Act . 10. The accused appeared on 03.05.2017 with his counsel, and was granted bail by this Court on the very same date. Pursuant to the grant of bail, the accused was directed to furnish requisite bail bonds, and accordingly, he had furnished his bail bonds and surety bonds which were accepted on 06.06.2017. Subsequently, upon satisfaction that a prima facie case existed warranting trial, this Court proceeded to frame notice under Section 251 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 ( CrPC ), which was duly served upon the accused on 03.11.2017. On being apprised of the substance of accusation, the accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. 11. Thereafter, despite being granted several opportunities by the Court to file an application under Section 145(2) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 for seeking permission to cross-examine the complainant, the accused failed to avail the same and did not comply with the directions of the Court in that regard. In view of the Page no.5/25 Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:34:52 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand persistent non-compliance and absence of any cogent justification, this Court was constrained to close the opportunity of the accused to cross-examine the complainant vide order dated 29.06.2018. Consequently, the matter was directed to proceed with the stage of defence evidence, affording the accused an opportunity to lead evidence in support of his case. 12. In support of his defence, the accused examined one witness, namely Ms. Anumita, who was produced as DW-1 and identified as a bank official. She entered the witness box and was duly examined-in-chief, followed by cross-examination by the learned counsel for the complainant. Upon completion of her testimony, she was formally discharged by the Court on 19.10.2022. The said witness was summoned by the accused ostensibly to support his plea regarding the nature of the bank transaction or account-related facts relevant to the disputed cheque. 13. That the accused subsequently moved an application under Section 311 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, seeking recall of the complainant for the purpose of cross-examination. Considering the principles of fair trial and in the interest of justice, the said application was allowed by this Court vide order dated 30.11.2022. In its order, the Court specifically granted the accused a final opportunity to cross-examine the complainant, and accordingly, the matter was reverted to the stage of complainant's evidence to facilitate compliance with the said direction. 14. In support of its case, the complainant led pre summoning evidence by examining its Authorised Representative (AR) as CW-1. The said witness, upon entering the witness box, expressly adopted and reaffirmed the contents of his pre-summoning evidence affidavit, Page no.6/25 Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:34:55 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand which had been tendered before this Court on 02.06.2016. The same was formally taken on record and treated as part of the complainant's post-summoning evidence. CW-1 relied upon the documents previously exhibited in support of the complaint and reiterated the facts concerning the sanction of the loan, execution of the loan agreement, issuance and dishonour of the cheque, as well as the service of legal notice and the accused's non-compliance thereof. 15. CW-1/15 earlier complaint 18. Ex. CW-1/16 Certified copy of return order dated 03.03.2015 16. Pursuant to the order dated 30.11.2022 allowing the recall of CW-1, the said witness was duly re-examined and cross-examined at length by the learned counsel for the accused. His testimony was concluded, and he was formally discharged by this Court on 08.02.2023. As the complainant opted not to examine any further witnesses, the complainant's evidence was accordingly closed. 17. Vide order dated 08.02.2023, the defence evidence was declared closed after the examination and discharge of DW-1, Ms. Anumita, who was the sole witness examined on behalf of the accused. No further defence witness was produced or sought to be summoned. Accordingly, the matter was listed for final arguments on the next date of hearing. 18. Upon a meticulous perusal of the record, it was observed by the learned Predecessor of this Court that the statement of the accused under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure had not been recorded at the appropriate stage. Inadvertently, the matter had proceeded directly with defence evidence and subsequently with final arguments, without affording the accused an opportunity to explain the incriminating circumstances appearing against him in the Page no.8/25 Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:35:02 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand prosecution's evidence. In view of this procedural lapse, the Court deemed it appropriate to rectify the irregularity, and accordingly, the statement of the accused was recorded thereafter on 23.01.2025, in compliance with the mandate of law. 19. During the said examination, the accused candidly admitted that he had indeed applied for a housing loan and had executed a loan agreement with the complainant company in the year 2011. He further admitted to having handed over 19 blank signed cheques to the complainant at the time of availing the loan, which he described as 'security cheques'. The accused further alleged that subsequent to the filing of the present complaint, the complainant also obtained two additional signed security cheques from him. 20. The accused claimed that he had already made part-payments amounting to approximately ₹3.5 to ₹4 lakhs towards the loan account. He alleged that the complainant had attempted to recover an amount in excess of what was actually due and had acted arbitrarily without furnishing any prior notice or intimation regarding the dues. While admitting his signature on the cheque in question, the accused categorically denied having filled in any of the other particulars on the said cheque. He also denied having received any legal demand notice from the complainant; however, he did acknowledge that the address mentioned in the legal notice corresponded to his correct residential address. Final arguments 21. Thereafter, this Court heard the final arguments advanced by both sides on 01.07.2025. The learned counsel for the complainant and the learned defence counsel were granted adequate opportunity to present Page no.9/25 Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:35:05 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand their respective submissions on facts as well as law, and the matter was reserved for judgment. 22. Learned counsel for the complainant has submitted that the accused has not disputed the factum of loan availed from the complainant company nor has he denied his signatures on the cheque in question. It is contended that the accused had availed a housing loan of ₹10,00,000/- and thereafter defaulted in repayment of installments despite repeated reminders and issuance of demand notice. Consequently, the cheque bearing no. 013354 dated 03.09.2012 for ₹9,39,030/-, which was issued by the accused towards discharge of his outstanding liability, was presented for encashment but dishonored for insufficiency of funds. 23. It is further submitted that after the dishonour of the cheque, a statutory legal notice dated 26.09.2012 was issued to the accused at his correct address and duly served, but the accused failed to make the payment within 15 days of service. Hence, the complainant was constrained to initiate the present proceedings under Section 138 NI Act. 24. Learned counsel has argued that the accused has failed to rebut the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act. It is submitted that the defence raised by the accused--namely that the cheque was a blank security cheque and that partial repayments had been made--are not supported by any cogent evidence. It is emphasized that the issuance of a cheque, even by way of security, does not absolve the accused if the cheque is presented against an existing liability, as held by way of catena of judgments. 25. The complainant further contends that the payments made after the dishonour of the cheque and filing of the complaint cannot nullify the criminal liability already incurred under Section 138 . Such payments, if any, may only be considered at the stage of sentencing. Digitally signed Page no.10/25 by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA Date: SHARMA 2025.07.31 16:35:08 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand 26. Lastly, it is argued that the complainant is a registered Housing Finance Company governed by the Reserve Bank of India, and is not subject to the local money lending laws such as the Punjab Registration of Money Lenders Act, 1938 . Hence, the defence of lack of license is not available to the accused. Learned counsel prays for conviction of the accused in accordance with law. 27. Per contra, learned counsel for the accused has submitted that the complainant has failed to discharge its burden of proving that the cheque in question was issued towards a legally enforceable debt. It is contended that the said cheque was one of 19 blank signed cheques which were handed over to the complainant at the time of disbursal of loan as security, and that the complainant has filled in an exaggerated amount without the consent of the accused. 28. Learned counsel argues that the accused had already repaid a substantial amount--approximately ₹3.5 to ₹4 lakhs--to the complainant, which was neither reflected in the complainant's ledger account nor disclosed to the Court. It is submitted that the complainant has selectively presented documents and suppressed material facts, thereby disentitling itself to any relief under Section 138 . 29. It is further submitted that the complainant company is engaged in money lending activities but does not possess any license under the Punjab Registration of Money Lenders Act, 1938 . In light of the Hon'ble Supreme Court's judgment in Rajender Anant Varik v. Govind Prabhugaonkar , it is argued that proceedings under Section 138 are not maintainable where the complainant has violated the statutory requirements of money lending regulations. 30. Learned counsel has also challenged the validity of service of legal notice. It is contended that the accused never received the demand notice allegedly sent by the complainant and hence the mandatory Page no.11/25 Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:35:11 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand requirement under the proviso to Section 138 NI Act stands unfulfilled. 31. Lastly, it is submitted that the complainant has failed to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt and that the accused, having already made considerable repayments, should not be made to suffer the rigours of criminal prosecution. A prayer is thus made for acquittal of the accused. Legal Analysis & Findings:- 32. I have heard at considerable length the detailed arguments advanced by the learned counsel appearing for the complainant as well as the learned counsel representing the accused. Their respective submissions have been carefully analysed in the context of the factual matrix and the legal principles applicable to the case. This Court has also undertaken a thorough and meticulous scrutiny of the entire judicial record, which includes the contents of the complaint, the affidavits and supporting documents annexed thereto, the oral testimonies of the complainant's and the defence witnesses recorded during the course of trial, and all exhibits relied upon by the respective parties. Each piece of evidence has been examined individually as well as in conjunction with the other evidence on record so as to assess its evidentiary value, credibility, and probative strength. The rival submissions have been objectively evaluated against the backdrop of the statutory framework and the well-settled legal position governing proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The Court has, therefore, endeavoured to reach a reasoned and just determination by adopting a holistic and balanced appreciation of the evidence and circumstances presented before it. 33. Before embarking upon a discussion on the merits of the present case, it is considered apposite to first delineate the legal framework governing the Page no.12/25 Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:35:14 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand offence of dishonour of cheque, as encapsulated under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The legislative intent behind enacting Section 138 is to instill greater financial discipline and sanctity in contractual obligations by deterring the issuance of cheques without sufficient funds or without adequate arrangements with the banker. The provision prescribes penal consequences in the event of dishonor of a cheque on grounds of insufficiency of funds or if the amount exceeds the arrangement with the bank, thereby recognizing the cheque as a legitimate instrument of payment in the eyes of the law. 34. In order to fasten criminal liability upon an accused under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, it is incumbent upon the complainant to plead and prove the existence of certain foundational ingredients through the averments made in the complaint and the evidence led during the course of trial. The essential ingredients that must be cumulatively satisfied are as follows: a. That the accused must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him with a banker, for the payment of a certain sum of money to another person, and such payment must have been intended for the discharge, in whole or in part, of a legally enforceable debt or other liability; b. That the said cheque must have been presented to the bank within a period of three months from the date on which it was drawn, or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; c. That upon such presentation, the cheque must have been returned unpaid by the bank, either due to insufficiency of funds in the drawer's account or because the amount exceeded the arrangement made by the drawer with the bank; d. That the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque must have issued a written statutory demand notice to the drawer, seeking payment of the cheque Page no.13/25 Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:35:17 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand amount, within 30 days from the date of receipt of information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque unpaid; e. That the drawer of the cheque, despite the receipt of such legal notice, failed to make payment of the cheque amount to the payee or holder in due course within 15 days from the date of such receipt. 35. Only upon proof of the aforementioned ingredients does the offence under Section 138 stand attracted, subject to the operation of statutory presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act. These presumptions, however, are rebuttable and impose a reverse burden upon the accused to dislodge the same on a preponderance of probabilities. 36. It is also pertinent to note that, as per the Explanation appended to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the expression "debt or other liability" refers exclusively to a legally enforceable debt or other liability. This legal clarification is of critical significance, as it makes clear that mere issuance of a cheque is not sufficient to attract penal liability under the statute. The dishonoured cheque must have been issued in discharge of a debt or liability which is subsisting and legally enforceable at the time of its issuance. A cheque issued as a gift, donation, or towards a time-barred or non-existent liability will not fall within the purview of Section 138 . Thus, the complainant must establish that at the time the cheque was drawn, there existed a valid and enforceable obligation in law for which the cheque was issued. 37. It is well-settled in law that the aforementioned ingredients must co-exist and be satisfied cumulatively in order to constitute the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The absence or non- fulfilment of even one of these statutory requirements is fatal to the prosecution's case and would disentitle the complainant from invoking penal liability against the drawer of the cheque. Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.14/25 SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:35:19 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand 38. The complainant's Authorised Representative stepped into the witness box as CW-1 and deposed on oath that the accused had approached the complainant company for a housing loan and was sanctioned a sum of ₹10,00,000/- vide sanction letter dated 24.05.2011 for the purpose of house renovation. He testified that the accused executed a loan agreement dated 02.06.2011 and issued several post-dated cheques, including the cheque in question bearing no. 013354 dated 03.09.2012 for ₹9,39,030/-, towards repayment of the outstanding loan amount. CW-1 further deposed that the cheque was presented for encashment through the complainant's banker, Punjab National Bank, Nehru Place Branch, New Delhi, but was returned dishonoured due to 'Funds Insufficient'. He affirmed that a legal demand notice dated 26.09.2012 was duly issued to the accused, which was served on 29.09.2012, but despite the lapse of the statutory period, the accused neither made the payment nor offered any response, thereby giving rise to the present cause of action under Section 138 of the NI Act. 39. During the course of his testimony, CW-1 further stated that all requisite documentation pertaining to the housing loan had been duly executed by the accused, including the loan application, sanction letter, loan agreement, and submission of post-dated cheques. He denied any deficiency in the record-keeping of the complainant company and clarified that the ledger account maintained in the regular course of business accurately reflected the outstanding dues against the accused as on 31.08.2012. CW-1 specifically asserted that the cheque in question was issued voluntarily by the accused in acknowledgment of his continuing liability under the loan account. He further deposed that upon presentation of the said cheque for encashment, it was returned unpaid by the drawee bank with the endorsement "Funds Insufficient," thereby confirming the accused's default. 40. During the course of his cross-examination, learned defence counsel made a concerted effort to impeach the credibility of CW-1 by highlighting alleged deficiencies in the documentation and questioning the mode of maintaining financial records. However, despite a detailed and exhaustive cross-examination, Page no.15/25 SHRUTI Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA 16:35:22 +0530 Date: 2025.07.31 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand the witness remained consistent, firm, and unwavering in his version of events. No material contradictions, inconsistencies, or damaging admissions could be extracted from the witness that would materially weaken or impeach the core of the complainant's case. The credibility of CW-1 thus remained intact, and his testimony continued to inspire confidence, particularly in light of the documentary evidence adduced in support thereof. 41. This Court finds the deposition of CW-1 to be cogent, consistent, and delivered in a manner that bears the hallmark of truth. Accordingly, the testimony of CW-1 inspires confidence and is found to be reliable, trustworthy, and worthy of full reliance. 42. Insofar as the statutory ingredients (b), (c), (d), and (e) under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act are concerned--namely, (b) the presentation of the cheque within its validity period, (c) its dishonour by the bank due to insufficiency of funds, (d) the issuance of a legal demand notice within 30 days of receiving intimation of dishonour, and (e) the drawer's failure to make payment within 15 days of receipt of the said notice--this Court finds that the complainant has successfully discharged the burden of proof in respect thereof. These facts stand duly established through unimpeached documentary evidence placed on record, which includes the original cheque , the cheque return memo dated 07.09.2012, the legal demand notice dated 26.09.2012, the postal receipts, acknowledgment card, and the online tracking report confirming service. There is no rebuttal to the presumption of service, and hence, the requirements under clauses (b) to (e) of Section 138 stand conclusively fulfilled. 43. It is also not in dispute that the accused failed to make payment of the cheque amount to the complainant within the statutory period of 15 days from the date of receipt of the legal demand notice. The record clearly reflects that the notice dated 26.09.2012 was duly served upon the accused, as evidenced by the acknowledgment cards and tracking report placed on record. Significantly, the Page no.16/25 Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:35:24 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand accused, during his statement under Section 313 CrPC, admitted that the address mentioned in the notice was correct, and did not specifically deny the receipt of the notice. Hence, service of the legal notice stands proved. Despite being afforded the statutory opportunity under the mandate of Section 138 of the NI Act, the accused did not tender the cheque amount within the prescribed period of 15 days, thereby fulfilling the last statutory condition for attracting penal liability under the said provision. 44. The Court shall now proceed to examine the most crucial ingredient under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, which constitutes the very foundation of the present prosecution--namely, whether the impugned cheque was issued by the accused in discharge of a legally enforceable debt or other liability. This aspect is of paramount significance, as the existence of such a liability is the sine qua non for attracting the statutory presumption under Section 139 of the NI Act. 45. In this background, this Court now undertakes a detailed and careful evaluation of the rival contentions and the evidence on record, to determine whether the said essential ingredient stands proved to the requisite standard in the present matter. 46. It is well-settled that once the complainant establishes that the cheque was drawn by the accused and that it was returned unpaid, a presumption arises under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Act that the cheque was issued for the discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability. The initial burden upon the complainant is merely to prove the foundational facts--namely, the execution and dishonour of the cheque. Once this is done, the burden shifts upon the accused to rebut the presumption. Such rebuttal may be established either by leading positive evidence or by pointing out inconsistencies, improbabilities, or material contradictions in the complainant's case, which may raise a reasonable doubt as to the existence of the alleged liability. Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHARMA SHRUTI Page no.17/25 SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:35:27 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand 47. For ready reference, the relevant provisions are reproduced as under:  Section 118(a) , NI Act - "Presumptions as to negotiable instruments: Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: (a) of consideration--that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration."  Section 139 , NI Act - "Presumption in favour of holder: It shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability." 48. This presumption, though statutory, is rebuttable in nature. The law places the initial evidentiary burden upon the accused to dislodge this presumption by raising a probable defence. It is now well-settled that the accused is not required to rebut the presumption beyond reasonable doubt; rather, the standard of rebuttal is that of preponderance of probabilities. The accused may discharge this burden either by adducing direct evidence or by relying on material inconsistencies, improbabilities, or contradictions in the complainant's case, elicited during cross- examination or otherwise. However, unless such rebuttal is successfully established, the presumption continues to operate in favour of the complainant. 49. This is a classic illustration of the principle of 'reverse onus' in operation, wherein the statutory scheme obligates the accused to rebut the presumption in favour of the complainant by leading what may be termed as 'negative evidence'. The accused is not required to affirmatively prove a particular fact; rather, he must bring on record material to demonstrate the non-existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. Since this reverse burden deviates from the general principle of criminal jurisprudence--namely, the presumption of innocence in favour of the accused-- the law has correspondingly tempered the standard of rebuttal. Recognising the inherent difficulty in leading negative evidence, the standard prescribed is not that of proof beyond reasonable doubt, but of preponderance of probabilities. As held by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Sangappa v. Mohan, (2010) 11 SCC 441, the accused need not conclusively disprove the existence of consideration or liability; it is sufficient if he can raise a probable defence which renders the existence of such liability doubtful or improbable in the mind of the Court. 51. In order to discharge the burden cast upon him under the reverse onus clause, the accused is required to either prove the non-existence of the alleged liability or demonstrate that the existence of such liability is so improbable or doubtful that a prudent person would conclude that no such obligation existed. This can be achieved by the accused either by leading direct evidence or relying upon circumstantial evidence in his defence. Alternatively, the accused may choose to effectively challenge the complainant's case by eliciting material contradictions or inconsistencies during cross-examination, thereby undermining the credibility of the prosecution's version. 52. If the accused succeeds in creating such a doubt, the burden then shifts back to the complainant, who must establish the existence of liability independent of the statutory presumptions. In such a scenario, the presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act would cease to operate in favour of the complainant and cannot be relied upon as conclusive proof. The complainant would then have to establish the liability on the strength of his own evidence. 53. In the light of the foregoing statutory provisions and the settled principles of law governing the operation and rebuttal of presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, this Court shall now proceed to critically examine the defence set up by the accused. The pivotal issue for Page no.19/25 Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:35:32 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand consideration at this stage is whether the defence raised by the accused is plausible, probable, and legally sustainable--such as would be sufficient to rebut the presumption regarding the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. 54. The defence may be founded either on direct evidence adduced by the accused or may emerge from material inconsistencies, omissions, or inherent improbabilities discernible within the complainant's version, particularly as elicited during cross-examination. However, to succeed, the defence must be cogent enough to inspire confidence and must raise a credible doubt regarding the true purpose behind the issuance of the impugned cheque. In this context, the Court now undertakes a holistic and careful analysis of the defence evidence on record, as well as the explanations tendered by the accused, to assess whether the statutory presumption stands effectively rebutted in the present case. 55. In his defence, the accused has put forth a plea that the cheque in question was not issued in discharge of any legally enforceable debt or liability owed to the complainant, but was rather one of several blank signed cheques handed over at the time of obtaining the housing loan purely as security. It is the specific case of the accused that he had taken a loan of ₹10,00,000/- from the complainant company in the year 2011 and had issued 19 blank signed cheques at the time of execution of the loan agreement. He further contended that he had already repaid a substantial portion of the loan amount--approximately ₹3.5 to ₹4 lakhs--through cash payments from time to time, and that the complainant has misused one such security cheque by filling in an exaggerated amount of ₹9,39,030/- and presenting the same without giving him any prior intimation. The accused has also referred to various cash receipts purportedly issued by the complainant, acknowledging partial payments made after dishonour of the cheque. 56. Upon a careful consideration of the defence set up by the accused, this Court finds the same to be wholly unsustainable, implausible, and unworthy of credence. At the outset, it is pertinent to note that the accused himself has Page no.20/25 Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:35:35 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand categorically admitted, during the course of his examination under Section 313 CrPC, that he had availed a housing loan of ₹10,00,000/- from the complainant company in the year 2011 and had executed the requisite loan documents in that regard. He further conceded that he had issued multiple cheques to the complainant, including the cheque in question, at the time of execution of the loan agreement. This express admission unequivocally affirms the existence of a commercial relationship between the parties. 57. The accused has attempted to dilute his admission by contending that the cheque was given merely as a 'security cheque'. However, this contention is bereft of merit. It is now a settled proposition of law that even if a cheque is issued by way of security, the moment such cheque is presented against a subsisting liability, and is returned unpaid due to insufficiency of funds or other reasons covered under Section 138 of the NI Act, the penal provisions are attracted. The character of the cheque as 'security' does not, by itself, absolve the drawer of liability once it is shown that a legally enforceable debt or liability existed on the date of its presentation. 58. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in Sripati Singh (Dead) through his daughter Ganga Singh v. State of Jharkhand & Anr., LL 2021 SC 606, has authoritatively clarified the legal position with respect to cheques issued as security. It was held that the mere nomenclature of a cheque as being issued by way of 'security' does not, by itself, preclude the invocation of penal consequences under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, provided that the said cheque was presented against a subsisting liability which had matured for repayment. The Hon'ble Court observed that when a cheque is issued as security with a stipulated time period for repayment, such cheque merely ensures that it cannot be presented before the maturity of the underlying obligation. However, in the absence of prior discharge of the debt or any altered arrangement between the parties, the cheque so issued remains validly enforceable against the outstanding liability. The Hon'ble Supreme Court further held that the availability of alternative modes of repayment does not nullify the legal consequences of dishonour under Section 138 if the drawer has failed to discharge the liability within the agreed period. It was categorically stated that there can be no rigid or inflexible rule that a security cheque can never be presented. If such a view were to be taken, the cheque would be reduced to the status of a mere promissory note, defeating the very object and purpose of the legislation. The Court observed that where a cheque --albeit issued as security--is presented against a legally enforceable debt and is dishonoured, the drawee has the lawful right to choose between initiating civil proceedings for recovery or prosecuting the drawer under the criminal provisions of the Act. 60. Applying the said principle to the facts of the present case, it is evident that the accused has not shown any material to prove that the underlying loan was discharged prior to the presentation of the cheque in question, nor has he demonstrated the existence of any altered arrangement precluding its presentation. In fact, he has admitted that a significant portion of the loan remained unpaid. Therefore, the presentation of the cheque cannot be said to be premature or unauthorised. In such a factual scenario, the defence that the cheque was merely issued as a security instrument is untenable and cannot absolve the accused from liability under Section 138 of the Act. 61. Though the accused has referred to certain alleged cash payments made subsequent to the dishonour of the cheque, and some of these entries have been elicited during the cross-examination of the complainant's witness and marked as Ex. X2 to X12, it is pertinent to observe that these payments were admittedly made after the date of dishonour of the cheque and after issuance of the statutory legal demand notice. It is a settled position in law that such subsequent payments, even if accepted to be true, do not absolve the drawer from the criminal liability that had already crystallized under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, Digitally signed Page no.22/25 by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA Date: SHARMA 2025.07.31 16:35:41 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand 1881, upon the failure to honour the cheque and make good the amount within the prescribed statutory period. 62. Section 138 contemplates strict adherence to the timeline post-dishonour, including service of a valid legal notice and the failure to make payment within 15 days thereof. Once the cause of action is complete, any payment thereafter, unless it results in a full and final settlement acknowledged by the complainant, has no bearing on the commission of the offence. In the present case, no such settlement has been pleaded or proved. 63. Moreover, the accused has failed to produce any coherent repayment statement, audited account, or even the testimony of an independent or neutral witness--such as a bank official, accountant, or representative of the complainant --to support the claim that the outstanding liability of ₹9,39,030/- was not due and payable at the time the cheque was presented. Mere vague assertions or scattered entries without corroboration or contextual explanation are insufficient to rebut the statutory presumption or dislodge the complainant's case, which rests on cogent documentary evidence including the loan ledger and legal notice correspondence. 64. The accused has further sought to challenge the very maintainability of the present complaint by alleging that the complainant company did not hold a valid license under the Punjab Registration of Money Lenders Act, 1938 , thereby suggesting that the loan transaction in question was illegal and unenforceable. In support of this contention, reliance has been placed on the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Rajender Anant Varik v. Govind B. Prabhugaonkar, SLP(C) No. 4728/2023, wherein it was held that a complaint by an unlicensed money lender was not maintainable under Section 138 of the NI Act. 65. This Court, however, finds no merit in the said contention. As is evident from the record, the complainant is a duly registered Housing Finance Company. It does not fall within the category of unregulated private money lenders Page no.23/25 Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.07.31 16:35:45 +0530 Ct case no. 630892/2016 M/s Vishwakriya Housing Finance Ltd. Vs. Hari Chand contemplated under the said 1938 Act. The complainant's status as a non-banking financial institution authorised to disburse housing loans is duly supported by documentary evidence including its registration and authorisation certificates. As such, the provisions of the Punjab Registration of Money Lenders Act have no application to a housing finance company operating under the framework of central financial regulation. 65. Furthermore, the judgment cited by the accused is clearly distinguishable on facts and law. That decision pertained to an individual who was engaged in money lending without a license, in contravention of the State Act. The Hon'ble Supreme Court, in that context, held that an unlicensed money lender could not maintain a complaint under Section 138 of the NI Act arising out of a void loan agreement. In the present case, however, the complainant is not only a registered legal entity, but is also subject to rigorous oversight and regulation by statutory authorities such as the NHB and the RBI. Accordingly, the ratio of the said judgment is not attracted to the facts of the present matter, and the defence raised by the accused on this ground stands rejected. 66. On a cumulative appreciation of the oral and documentary evidence adduced by both sides, and the admissions made by the accused, it stands conclusively proved that the cheque in question was issued by the accused towards a legally enforceable debt, was dishonoured for insufficiency of funds, and despite service of a valid legal notice, the accused failed to make payment within the stipulated period. The defence raised by the accused is illusory, lacks documentary corroboration, and fails to rebut the statutory presumption in favour of the complainant. All the essential ingredients of the offence under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 stand satisfied. Conclusion 67. In the light of the aforementioned discussion, the complainant has successfully proved all the ingredients of Section 138 NI Act.
